Effective sample sizes of the MCMC samples of the random effects

Source: R/mcmc_diagnostics.R
summarise_mcmc.Rd

Computes the effective sample size of the Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) samples of the random effects stored in a fitted binomial, Poisson or negative binomial model, for the mean of the spatial random effects over the locations, for the spatial random effect at each location and for each level of every unstructured random effect.

Usage

summarise_mcmc(object)

Arguments

object

A fitted RiskMap object returned by glgpm() for a binomial, Poisson or negative binomial model with return_samples = TRUE.

Value

A tibble with one row per chain and columns

effect

"mean of S" for the mean of the spatial random effects over the locations, "S" for the spatial random effect at a location, or the name of the variable of an unstructured random effect.

component

The location, numbered as the rows of object$coords, or the level of the random effect, numbered as in object$re. It is NA for the mean.

ess

The effective sample size.

The number of samples is stored in the attribute "n_samples".

Details

The samples are those drawn by glgpm() at the fitted parameter values, which are used for the fitted values and for spatial prediction. When the model has a nugget, the spatial random effect at a location includes it.

The effective sample size of a chain is the number of independent draws that would estimate the mean of its target distribution as precisely as the correlated MCMC samples do. It is the number of samples divided by the integrated autocorrelation time, \(1 + 2 \sum_{k \ge 1} \rho_k\), where \(\rho_k\) is the autocorrelation at lag \(k\). The sum is estimated with the initial monotone sequence estimator of Geyer (1992), which adds pairs of consecutive sample autocorrelations while their sum is positive and forces these sums to decrease. As in Stan, the autocorrelation time is not allowed to fall below \(1 / \log_{10} N\) for \(N\) samples, so the effective sample size of an antithetic chain is at most \(N \log_{10} N\). A chain that never moves has an effective sample size of zero.

References

Geyer, C. J. (1992). Practical Markov chain Monte Carlo. Statistical Science, 7(4), 473-483.

See also

plot_mcmc()

Examples

# \donttest{
data(liberia)
liberia <- sf::st_as_sf(liberia, coords = c("long", "lat"), crs = 4326)
fit <- glgpm(npos ~ log(elevation) + gp(), denominator = ntest,
             data = liberia, model_crs = 32629, family = "binomial",
             messages = FALSE)
ess <- summarise_mcmc(fit)
# The mean and the five locations with the smallest effective sample size
ess[1, ]
#> # A tibble: 1 × 3
#>   effect    component   ess
#>   <chr>         <int> <dbl>
#> 1 mean of S        NA 1294.
head(ess[order(ess$ess), ], 5)
#> # A tibble: 5 × 3
#>   effect    component   ess
#>   <chr>         <int> <dbl>
#> 1 mean of S        NA 1294.
#> 2 S                44 1325.
#> 3 S                28 1337.
#> 4 S                56 1338.
#> 5 S                53 1352.
# }
